title: Anxiety and sorrow
hookLine: O Allah, I seek refuge from worry and grief, weakness and laziness, debt and being overpowered (Bukhari)
tomorrow: what did the Prophet ﷺ say when everything went wrong?

cards: Three tabs open at one in the morning: a bill, a list of things to pack, an old photo from home. One is about what's owed. One is about what's coming.
One is about what's gone. Worry and grief can sit on the chest like the same weight. So, one question for today: are they the same thing?
A line the Prophet ﷺ said often answers no, and names them apart, in pairs.

teach.b: In Sahih al-Bukhari, the line goes: O Allah, I seek refuge in You from worry and grief, from weakness and laziness, from miserliness and cowardice, from the weight of debt and from being overpowered by others.
Some scholars explain the first pair this way: hamm, worry, is about what hasn't happened yet; hazan, grief, is about what already has. One faces forward, one faces back.
Then weakness, which can't, and laziness, which won't. Debt, which presses from outside; being overpowered, which pins you down.

Each pair is a matched set, so no door is left open behind the one you closed. Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: the line doesn't pretend you won't feel any of it. It names it, precisely, and asks for refuge.
Now a neighbor who speaks to the forward-facing half.

In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says, in the King James words: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof."
Shared: both refuse to let tomorrow run the house.

And one honest difference: Matthew's verse is a teaching about where to set the mind, today and not tomorrow; the hadith is a request, said to God, that names worry and grief apart and asks refuge from each.
Neither is the other in a different coat.

how: Muslims say this line from the hadith in moments of worry, and some include it in the morning and evening remembrances.

o: a hymn of mourning sung after a funeral
a vow to stop worrying, made at the new year
asking God's refuge from worry and grief, named apart

games.q: the pairs, paired — tap the pairs.

s: the hadith treats worry and grief as one feeling
it names them separately, as a pair; some scholars explain one faces ahead, one behind.
Matthew 6:34 says each day has trouble enough of its own
sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof, in the King James words.
the line promises you'll never feel worry again
it names worry and asks refuge from it; it doesn't pretend it won't come.

games.q: Jordan asks: 'so your prayer and my verse are basically the same, right?' what's the fair answer?
o: yes, exactly; every religion teaches the same thing about worry.
alike in refusing to let worry rule; different in shape: a teaching, and a request.
no, they have nothing at all to do with each other.
games.why: both set worry down. Matthew teaches where to set the mind; the hadith asks God's refuge, naming worry and grief apart.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write two words as headings: ahead, and behind. Under 'ahead', one thing you're worried about; under 'behind', one thing you're grieving, even a small one. Look at them as two different weights, not one.
If you pray, say the line's first words over both: I seek refuge in You from worry and grief.

wordCard.voice: Anxiety and sorrow: a line from the hadith asking refuge from worry and grief, and the troubles that come with them, in pairs.

orig.note: Arabic: worry (hamm) and grief (hazan), the line's first pair.

carryVoice: Keep it near: refuge from worry, for ahead and behind are different weights, and both can be handed over. Named, and set down.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 6369 (refuge from worry and grief; also 6363)
